notes.1a: Most candidates scored credit on this question. The most common error was to identify the separating/tap funnel as a burette or thistle funnel. Most candidates recognised the flask though some mistakenly thought it was a beaker. Gas jar or measuring cylinder was allowed for the container collecting the gas. This container was sometimes labelled as a collecting tube, glass jar or cylinder.
notes.1b: Generally well answered. The collection of the gas by upward delivery was recognised by most candidates.
notes.1c: Only the more able candidates realised that the passage of the gas through the acid would dry it or remove impurities. Some vague answers referred to observing bubbles and acidifying the gas.
notes.3a: The table of results was generally completed correctly.
notes.3b: Most candidates successfully plotted the results and drew a smooth curve. A minority of candidates omitted the origin and then drew a distorted graph through the inaccurate point.
notes.3c: Vague descriptions such as ‘the second one’ were penalised. Some candidates drew the curve through the two minute point and then identified the one minute point as inaccurate – this was penalised.
notes.3d: The sketches were generally steeper than the original curve as required. However, many sketches did not level out at the same level as the original curve.
notes.4a: and (b) The tables of results were usually completed correctly.
notes.4c: Some candidates misread the scale on the y-axis. Many smooth line graphs were not smooth. Thick, wobbly and multiple lines were common.
notes.4d: A minority of candidates used experiment 2 instead of experiment 1. Some answers showed no indication as to how the answer had been obtained and some misread the scale on the x-axis.
notes.4e: Vague references to the reactivity of the acids and different acidity were prevalent. Good answers included the idea of more particle collisions.
notes.4g: Credit was given for realising that the reaction had finished and that the temperature would return to room temperature/23 C. Poor answers lacked detail and discussed either the temperature remaining constant or decreasing to 0 C.
notes.5c: The formation of white precipitates and their soluble or insoluble nature was recognised by most candidates.
notes.5d: The formation of water or recognition of a hydrated or hydrous(sic) salt was only understood by a minority of candidates.
notes.5f: A good discriminating question. Credit was given for the identification of the nitrate ion and realising that the salt was hydrated. Too many candidates referred to the presence of ammonia or ammonium instead of the nitrate ion. A significant number of candidates identified the presence of a sulfate even though the tests showed that a sulfate was absent.
notes.6a: Some candidates placed the arrow beneath the tube in the beaker of ice. The arrow was expected to be drawn below the solid in the horizontally placed tube. Frequently this question was not attempted.
notes.6b: The common incorrect answers were blue to pink or confusion with hydrated copper sulfate i.e. blue to white.
notes.6c: Generally well answered, though some candidates described the cooling/condensing of crystals/solid.
notes.6d: References to gases/air entering the tube scored no credit. The idea of relieving pressure or allowing gases to escape scored credit. Named incorrect gases, e.g. chlorine/hydrogen. escaping from the apparatus were penalised.
